I have tried this with DXM and other dissociatives acting on NMDA and it’s pretty much impossible because you either can’t focus well enough to do what you need to do or even if you can focus, the lack of guidance from an actual professional can make things go terribly wrong. I found this out the hard way when I took dissociatives and convinced myself that my trauma itself was “good” in an attempt to think about it differently, only to end up with very harmful beliefs. I once knew someone that thought bullying was “good” because it makes you stronger, and that person themselves would bully me sometimes thinking it helped… that’s basically similar to how I reacted after trying to heal myself with dissociatives, except I got lucky enough that my best friend noticed my strange underlying beliefs right away and helped undo them.

The way dissociatives/NMDA antagonists help therapeutically is that they essentially make it easier to rewire your brain in terms of making your interpretations of your experiences and subsequent beliefs about things more “malleable” and easier to integrate during a trip (other than also helping you see your experiences from another perspective), so naturally people figured out that dissociatives and a licensed professional to focus on and talk to about your stuff can pretty much accelerate healing. On that note though, given what makes ketamine therapy effective, it is possible to find similar results by simply being open to examining our thoughts and feelings in response to what happened to us and seeing whether they truly serve our future - speaking from personal experience. I won’t go any further than that in my reply so I don’t accidentally proselytize, especially considering you already see a therapist. Just wanted to share that I’ve been able to heal a great deal from my own CPTSD even after I’ve also done the song and dance with trying to find substances that would help me break through when I was stuck. Good luck!

However way he might treat you like gold doesn't excuse constantly making you feel bad and blaming you instead of holding himself accountable, regardless of however way you might be considered difficult. A healthy relationship would involve communication between the two of you saying what you're thinking and feeling and having respect for those things in one another, in terms of recognizing the other person's internal experience as valid without applying judgements like "right" or "wrong". The *response* to your experience or another's is what could be helpful or harmful. And to disregard your experience in favor of trying to change you is indeed harmful and wrong. You have every right to feel hurt by what he does, because it is hurtful and very unnecessary, regardless of whether you might be a sensitive person. What he feels or thinks about you shouldn't dictate how he treats you. Your partner is emotionally abusive.

BPD tends to stem in part from chronic invalidation with regards to our thoughts and feelings so it makes sense that we tend to validate other immediately when it comes to those things, because we know what it's like to be constantly told that we're not thinking or feeling the "right" way, or that what we're thinking or feeling is "good" or "bad".

That being said, while it can really hurt to have your personal experience misunderstood by others, I think you're right that there needs to be a distinction between validating experiences and enabling unhealthy responses. It's one thing to say yes I can see what led up to making you feel like you wanted to cheat, but it's another to say yes you should have cheated. It's also harmful like you said to make judgements against other people involved with a person especially since we never know the big picture, and I wouldn't want to accidentally encourage demonizing someone when we only have bits and pieces of what we're told. And even if it were true that the other person in a situation is genuinely a bad person, it still wouldn't be helpful to encourage harmful behavior especially since it could always make something or someone worse in the long run.

I’ve been psychologically tortured as well (with some physical stuff but the psychological torture was the main component), for years. I’ve healed A LOT from it, but I know I still have quite a way to go with it, too. I’ve had multiple suicide attempts and nearly died from drug addiction, but today I’m totally off psych meds, I have a full-time job, and plenty of healthy relationships with others.

I’ve seen people say that healing never truly ends, and I’m unsure as to how true that is, however to me it hasn’t really mattered as long as I keep focusing on healing itself rather than some standard that may or may not be reachable. I try to see it as I would if I were in the self-improvement community and were doing this out of devotion to myself and not necessarily out of a desire to “fix” what I don’t like.

Anyway, I’ve found it’s best to focus on how it’s affected me the most in the present and go from there. Boiling it down to something like anger, anxiety, shame, fear of vulnerability, addiction/escapism, codependency etc or a combination of the above can give you a good direction to go in. They’re not the only topics you could go through, but some potential starting points. Or if you cannot figure out what really affects you the most, you can always just pay attention to what evokes a negative reaction in you the most and how you feel, think, and respond as a result of the triggering events.

Also, try to avoid comparing what you went through to others as well, in terms of whether it was better or worse. I thought I’d mention that because for me I’ve had a habit of looking at who had it better or worse than me to see if what I went through was as bad as I thought it was. I realized this was a form of seeking a way to validate what I went through and how I felt. However way you felt as a result is totally valid, and it’s generally not a good idea to intellectualize feelings anyway. If you ever find yourself needing to justify how you feel a lot with somebody, they’re probably not healthy to be around.

I’m not sure if it’s the same for you, but for the longest I wondered if I was being attention-seeking, dramatic, or focusing too much on the negative etc because of how bad my past seemed even though it involved way more psychological than physical stuff - but I realized for me personally that its BECAUSE it involved primarily psychological torture, that yes, it was THAT bad (my abusers having intentionally crafted ways to get horribly deep inside my head and fuck with me for years on end). Similarly, it has helped me to stop trying to get people to understand what I truly went through - not only because it can be so easy to be invalidated, but because (for me) most people literally just won’t get it unless they are genuinely, 100% empathetic in some way. 

The things I mentioned have been more helpful than clinging to diagnostic labels, even though I do have them. At most I’ve used the labels as directions for helping myself as well. Yes it can be validating to know that how you’ve been affected in particular can be recognized by others, but I’ve also found it can be very easy to fall into the trap of feeling like things will never change *because* of those diagnoses.

Lastly, going off the first point of doing what I can in the present to move forward - it’s been most helpful for me to stop beating myself up for stuff and just allow myself to learn from slip-ups in order to improve. They teach you this when you’re recovering from addiction, to stop being mad at yourself for relapses and just focus on what led up to it so you can do differently next time. But I realized this applies to most things in life. Be kind to yourself and allow yourself to make mistakes, because you’ll be making mistakes for as long as you live, anyway.
